name: Guaraní
info: The Guaraní are culturally related Indigenous peoples of South America, distinguished by the Guarani language, whose traditional range lies in Paraguay, Misiones, southern Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia, and who number around 280,000 today.

facts.homeland: Traditionally the land between the Paraná River and the lower Paraguay River in what is now Paraguay, the Misiones Province of Argentina, southern Brazil once as far east as Rio de Janeiro, and parts of Uruguay and Bolivia; today mainly Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay, with the Eastern Bolivian Guarani in the Gran Chaco near the Pilcomayo River
facts.period: First encountered by Europeans in the early 16th century; the Jesuit missions from 1610 until the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767; the Guarani War of 1754–1756; the Bolivian Chiriguanos resisting until the Battle of Kuruyuki in 1892; a living people today
facts.known: the Guarani language, an official language of Paraguay and Bolivia; communal houses (malocas); the Jesuit missions, which held more than 100,000 people; the mission army that defeated the Paulista slave raiders in 1641; the Guarani War against the Treaty of Madrid; myths of Ñamandu, Tupã and the Pombero
facts.sources: Spanish and Jesuit records, among them Antonio Ruiz de Montoya’s The Spiritual Conquest and the accounts of Martin Dobrizhoffer; letters such as Francisco González de Paniagua’s of 1545 and the caciques of San Luis’s of 1768; mission censuses; myths compiled by the Universidad Nacional de Misiones; modern historians such as Barbara Ganson

t: Before they met Europeans the Guarani called themselves Abá, “men” or “people”; the name Guarani was first applied by Jesuit missionaries to those who had accepted Christianity.
Paulista slave raiders destroyed most of the early Jesuit missions, and within two years 60,000 converts were carried off for sale to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
The Guarani language is an official language of Paraguay and Bolivia, and as of 2012 an estimated 90% of the people in Paraguay spoke it.
dyk: When an 800-strong Paulista army attacked the missions in 1641, it was met on the Acaray River by Christian Guarani armed with guns, and its defeat in two battles warded off invasions for ten years.
ev: Aracare, a chief from the Jejuy River, was hanged by the Spanish, prompting an unsuccessful rebellion by Tabare
Loreto, the first Jesuit mission of Guayrá, was founded on the Paranapanema
Paulistas burned the San Antonio mission, killed many and carried the rest into slavery
A Guarani army armed with guns defeated the Paulistas in two battles on the Acaray River
The 30 Guarani missions held 141,252 converts, guarded by an army of 7,000 Guaranis
The Guarani fought for their land against the Treaty of Madrid in the Guarani War
The Jesuits were expelled from Spanish dominions, and the missions soon declined
The Chiriguanos led by Apiaguaiki Tumpa were defeated in the Battle of Kuruyuki

sections.origins:
The Guaraní are a group of culturally related Indigenous peoples of South America, distinguished from the related Tupi by their use of the Guarani language. Their traditional range lies in what is now Paraguay between the Paraná River and the lower Paraguay River, the Misiones Province of Argentina, southern Brazil once as far east as Rio de Janeiro, and parts of Uruguay and Bolivia.

The history and meaning of the name are disputed. Before they encountered Europeans the Guarani called themselves simply Abá, meaning “men” or “people”. Early Jesuit missionaries first applied the term Guarani to those who had accepted conversion to Christianity, and used Cayua or Caingua, roughly “the ones from the jungle”, for those who refused it. Barbara Ganson writes that the Spanish gave the name because it means “warrior” in the Tupi-Guaraní dialect spoken there, and Guarinĩ is attested in 16th-century Old Tupi as “war, warrior, to wage war, warlord”. Today the name is extended to all people of native origin, whatever their place in society.
sections.society:
Early Guarani villages often consisted of communal houses, malocas or ocas, each housing several families under the leadership of a chief. Communities were united by common interest and language and tended to form tribal groups by dialect. It is estimated that the Guarani numbered some 400,000 people when Europeans first met them. They were then sedentary and agricultural, living largely on manioc, maize, wild game and honey. Polygamy was practised, and captives were eaten.

The Guaraní in Bolivia, called Chiriguanos, lived in the foothills of the Andes and had a history of their own. Today the Eastern Bolivian Guarani live in the Gran Chaco near the Pilcomayo River, close to the Paraguayan and Argentine borders, in three principal subgroups: around fifty thousand Ava Guarani, chiefly in the Andean foothills; the Simba Guarani near the Pilcomayo, known for the braided hair men once wore; and the Izoceño Guarani of Izozog on the Parapetí River. They are represented by the Assembly of the Guarani People and keep a justice system of their own beside ordinary law, aimed at reconciliation and communal peace.
sections.beliefs:
Little is known of early Guarani beliefs. They practised a form of animistic pantheism, much of which survives in folklore and myth, and Guarani mythology is still widespread in rural Paraguay. The Jesuit Martin Dobrizhoffer wrote that they had once practised cannibalism, perhaps as a funerary rite, but later laid the dead in large jars placed upside down in the ground.

In the cosmogonic myths, creation and destruction are dictated by Ñamandu, “the true father, the first one”, followed by a pantheon of gods led by Yporú, better known as Tupã. Jasy rules the night, while Aña is a malign deity at the bottom of the Iguazu River. Animistic stories tell of people turned into animals, plants and minerals: Ka’a Jarýi became the sacred herb yerba, and Irupé the giant lily. The Pombero are forest spirits who must be appeased with gifts such as honey; among them are Jasy Jatere and Kuarahy Jára, protector of birds. The Iguazu Falls are sacred to the Guarani and the setting of many legends.
sections.arts:
The Guarani language is the people’s best-known creation and inheritance. Early in the history of Asunción the Franciscan Luis de Bolaños translated the catechism into Guarani, and the language became the medium of mission life. Today Standard Paraguayan Guarani is flourishing in Paraguay, where children learn it both at home and in public schools, and it is taught in 12 countries. Other peoples of the Paraguayan Chaco and northern Argentina also used it, and Paraguayan migration has carried it to Argentina and Spain.

Guarani oral literature survives in a large body of myths and legends. The Universidad Nacional de Misiones compiled them as Myths and Legends: A Journey around the Guarani Lands, an anthology first published in 1870 and translated into English in 1906. They range from the creation of the world to stories of the hummingbird Mainumby, which carries good spirits from flowers back to Tupã, and of glowworms and butterflies as the reborn spirits of people. Many Guarani place names remain across Bolivia, among them Yacuiba, Tatarenda, Saipurú, Abapó and Urubichá.
sections.exchange:
After the defeat of Juan Diaz de Solis’s expedition in 1516, survivors led by Alejo Garcia went inland with a Guarani band, and Asunción was founded after 1537. The early alliance custom of cuñadazgo, by which caciques gave women to newcomers, was supplanted after 1541 by the rancheadas, mass seizures of women who were bought, sold and exported as slaves; modern historians describe this as sexual and economic coercion. In 1542 the Spanish hanged the chief Aracare, and Tabare’s rebellion failed. Slave hunters based in São Paulo captured and sold many Guaranis, who had only bows and arrows against them.

Jesuit missions from 1610 offered the only real protection against enslavement, but Paulista raiders burned them and carried 60,000 converts off for sale. Armed with guns by royal permission, a Guarani army beat the raiders in 1641. Smallpox killed about 30,000 two years after 1732, and about 12,000 more in 1765. The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 ordered the Guarani off their land without consulting them, and the Guarani War killed thousands. After the Jesuits’ expulsion in 1767 the missions fell apart; by 1814 the mission Indians numbered 8,000.
sections.legacy:
The Guarani people and culture persist. In Paraguay Guarani lineage predominates in the population, many are descendants of mission exiles, and the language is spoken in most departments; it is one of the country’s two official languages beside Spanish, and an official language of Bolivia too. In modern Spanish, Guaraní can also mean any Paraguayan. Their demographic dominance of the region has nevertheless been reduced by colonisation and the rise of mestizos, and the Guarani number around 280,000 today.

The missions left lasting marks: a 2018 study found that educational attainment remains 10–15% higher, and incomes about 10% higher, in areas of former Jesuit presence within the Guarani area. In Argentina Guarani communities defend their ancestral lands against illegal logging and government neglect, and a group called Los Rumberos, “The Patrollers”, guards the forest. Remembered figures include Juliana, a 16th-century woman who killed her Spanish master; Sepé Tiarayú, a leader of the Guarani War venerated as a saint in Brazil and Argentina; and Andrés Guazurary, governor of Misiones.

summary: The Guaraní are Indigenous peoples of South America, once sedentary farmers of manioc and maize between the Paraná and Paraguay rivers. They endured enslavement by Spanish settlers and Paulista raiders, lived in large numbers in the Jesuit missions, fought the Guarani War, and today number around 280,000, their language official in Paraguay and Bolivia.
references: Ganson, Barbara Anne, The Guaraní under Spanish rule in the Río de la Plata (Stanford University Press, 2003)
Combès, Isabelle; Lowrey, Kathleen, “Slaves without Masters? Arawakan Dynasties among the Chiriguano (Bolivian Chaco, Sixteenth to Twentieth Centuries)”, Ethnohistory 53 (4) (2006)
Salvo, Rosita Escalada; Zamboni, Olga, Myths and Legends: A Journey around the Guarani Lands – Anthology (Editorial Universitaria, Universidad Nacional de Misiones, 2004)

notes: start 1516 is only the first European contact the article dates (Solis’s defeat); the article gives no date for the people’s origins. The editor may prefer another start.

The article says the Universidad Nacional de Misiones anthology was published ‘in 1870’, which conflicts with a modern university; kept as the article gives it (the reference says first published 1870).
The article’s treaty dates conflict: ‘Seven years of guerrilla warfare’ against the war of 1754–1756; I used 1754–1756.
Left out: the article’s statement that the Chiriguanos were ‘warlike’ and ‘pacified’ (colonisers’ terms); the death penalty in Bolivian Guarani justice; Kurupi details.
